opus-5.5.text:
Jensen is a very unique leader. The first thing that strikes you is how deeply technical he is. He's the CEO of a company with tens of thousands of people, but when you present research to him, he goes straight to the core: what's the fundamental problem, why does it matter, and what would it take to really solve it. You can't hide behind buzzwords with him. He wants first principles.

The second thing is his long-term vision. Many things NVIDIA is known for today, like CUDA, the bet on deep learning, and now physical AI and robotics, started as investments years before the market was ready. He's willing to stay patient for a decade if he believes a direction is right. For a researcher, that's incredibly empowering, because you're not being pushed to show a quarterly result. You're encouraged to go after problems that might take many years.

He's also very hands-on and fast. He reads a lot, he asks a lot of questions, and he expects people to move quickly. The organization is quite flat. He has many direct reports, and information flows to him directly rather than through layers of management. That means you need to be clear and honest about where things stand, including what isn't working.

And I'd say he has a very strong sense of mission. He often talks about doing things that only NVIDIA can do, problems that are really hard and where we can make a unique contribution, rather than competing in crowded spaces. That philosophy shapes how we pick research directions. For my team, working on generative AI and world models like Cosmos, it came from that same thinking: if AI is going to enter the physical world, someone needs to build the foundation for it, and we should be the ones to do it.

So, technical, visionary, demanding, but also very supportive of people who are passionate about solving hard problems. That combination is quite rare.

fable-5.1.text:
Jensen is, first of all, someone who is extremely demanding, but demanding in a way that comes from how much he cares about the work. He pays attention to details that you wouldn't expect a CEO of a company that size to notice. He'll read a research paper our team put out, and then he'll ask you a very specific question about why we made a particular design choice. So you can't be sloppy around him. You have to really know your stuff.

The second thing I'd say is that he has a very long time horizon. When we started the generative AI research effort at NVIDIA, a lot of the things we were doing didn't have an obvious product attached to them. He supported it anyway, because he believed computing was going to change and that NVIDIA needed to be building the foundation before it was obvious to everyone else. That kind of patience, combined with the intensity, is a rare combination.

The third thing is that he's a teacher. In meetings he'll often stop and explain his reasoning, not just give a decision. He wants people to understand how he's thinking about the problem so they can make the same kind of judgment themselves. I've learned a great deal from him about how to think about technology, about markets, about where the puck is going.

And honestly, he's very direct. If something isn't good enough, he'll tell you. It can be uncomfortable, but it's never personal. It's always about making the work better. Over time you come to appreciate that, because you always know where you stand.
